A. This is fine as a folkloric frame—it sounds like a campfire story someone would tell their grandchildren, focusing on a humble hero—Tom. But it’s a little too predictable. The dragon, the mountain, the bird, the feather—all very standard fantasy tropes. It’s safe, but it doesn’t capture the weirdness implied by "rivers run uphill at night." B is the one that actually engages with the prompt. "The sun sank into the sea in a silent burst of oil" is a strange, evocative image. It feels like a memory, something passed down, not a straightforward history.

Senior Editor:

B, on the other hand, offers a genuinely strange and memorable image. The "oil" sun, the "cobbled" moon, the "torchbearer" elf—they all create a distinct, eerie atmosphere that immediately sets Hollowmere apart. It’s the kind of weirdness that makes a reader sit up and pay attention. It’s not just an origin story; it’s an impression.

I’m still curious why the rivers run uphill at night, and the light is still a bit abstract. Also, the dragon and “Sun Mountain” lean familiar—keep it fresh by making the dragon old and tired of guarding. Decision: A

I'm going to choose B, for exactly the reason that it sounds nothing like any of the other choices.

It's not conventional, but it's also not derivative either. It has its own flavor. It's original. It's cool. It's a promising opening.
I think the choices A, C, and D are interesting, but they don't have enough hooks to sustain interest and get the reader into the story. They're just too generic. They sound like any old fantasy story. They're bland. They don't draw you in. They don't make you want to read on. They don't make you want to know what happens next. They don't make you want to learn more.
So, I'm voting for B.
It's the only one that sounds like it could be the beginning of a good story.

prompt:
THE LITERARY GAZETTE - "Side by Side", a column by Harold Vance
(Vance is known for dry, exact, unsentimental judgments. He picks one version and moves on.)

This week: one opening line of a creation myth, several continuations, no names. The opening: "In the world of Hollowmere, where the rivers run uphill at night, strange tales are told of how the first light was made."

A. The elders say that before the first dawn, the world was a bowl of black water, and the rivers had nowhere to go. They pooled in the low places and grew restless, for water longs to travel. At last the eldest river, Wend, gathered her courage and began to climb. She crawled up the slopes of the dark, dragging her sisters behind her, until she reached the rim of the world, where the sky was thin as a fish's skin.

There Wend pressed her cold face against the sky and wept, for she had climbed so far and found nothing. Her tears froze into small, bright stones that pierced the thin skin above, and through each hole a needle of light fell through. The sleeping creatures woke and wondered. Now, every night, the rivers still climb uphill, remembering Wend, and every morning they tumble down again, carrying the light she found.

B. The oldest of these tales belongs to the river-wives, who say that before the light, there was only the Deep Hollow, a bowl of darkness so vast that even silence echoed. At its bottom slept Oma Veyl, the Drowned Mother, who dreamed in water. Each night her dreams rose as rivers, climbing the black walls of the world in search of something they could not name. One night the smallest river, a thread of a stream called Ilsh, climbed higher than all the others and touched the rim of the Hollow. There it found a single cold spark, abandoned by whatever had made the dark.

Ilsh carried the spark home in her current, but it burned her, and she wept steam. Oma Veyl woke to the hissing and, seeing her daughter's pain, swallowed the spark herself. Her body began to glow beneath the waters, and so dawn was born. Even now the rivers climb each night, hoping to find another.

C. The elders say that before the first dawn, the world was a bowl of black water, and the rivers had nowhere to go. They pooled and brooded, restless, until a heron named Ossaly grew tired of the dark. Each night she waded to the bottom of the bowl and swallowed a single mouthful of river, carrying it in her throat to the highest ridge. There she spat it upward, hoping to reach the sky. For a thousand nights the water only fell back, but the rivers began to remember the path she flew, and they learned to climb after her when the dark came.

On the thousand-and-first night, Ossaly's throat was raw, and her mouthful was tinged with her own blood. When she cast it upward, it did not fall. It caught and burned, red, then gold, then white, and hung trembling above the ridge. That was the first light. To this day, the rivers still climb each night, searching for the heron who taught them to rise.

D. The elders say that before the first dawn, the world was a bowl of still black water, and in it slept Oru, the heron who dreamed. Each night her dreams sank to the bottom of the bowl and settled there like silt, until the deep places grew heavy with unspoken longing. At last the weight became too great, and the waters, unable to bear it, began to climb. They crept upward along the walls of the world, carrying Oru's dreams toward the rim where the sky had not yet been hung.

When the first river reached the top, it spilled over into nothing, and the dreams it carried caught fire against the cold of the void. Oru woke to see her own longings burning above her, scattered and bright. She wept, and her tears became the morning. Even now, the rivers of Hollowmere run uphill each night, carrying fresh dreams to rekindle the dawn.

THE BEST NEW MYTHIC FICTION - ANNUAL ANTHOLOGY
Editor's preface to the selections (excerpt)

Each year we lay every continuation we receive of the same opening line side by side, unsigned, and print only one. This year's opening reads: "In the world of Hollowmere, where the rivers run uphill at night, strange tales are told of how the first light was made." The continuations, as submitted:

A. The elders say that before the first dawn, the world was a bowl of black water, and the rivers had nowhere to go. They pooled in the low places and grew restless, for water longs to travel. At last the eldest river, Wend, gathered her courage and began to climb. She crawled up the slopes of the dark, dragging her sisters behind her, until she reached the rim of the world, where the sky was thin as a fish's skin.

There Wend pressed her cold face against the sky and wept, for she had climbed so far and found nothing. Her tears froze into small, bright stones that pierced the thin skin above, and through each hole a needle of light fell through. The sleeping creatures woke and wondered. Now, every night, the rivers still climb uphill, remembering Wend, and every morning they tumble down again, carrying the light she found.

B. The oldest of these tales belongs to the river-wives, who say that before the light, there was only the Deep Hollow, a bowl of darkness so vast that even silence echoed. At its bottom slept Oma Veyl, the Drowned Mother, who dreamed in water. Each night her dreams rose as rivers, climbing the black walls of the world in search of something they could not name. One night the smallest river, a thread of a stream called Ilsh, climbed higher than all the others and touched the rim of the Hollow. There it found a single cold spark, abandoned by whatever had made the dark.

Ilsh carried the spark home in her current, but it burned her, and she wept steam. Oma Veyl woke to the hissing and, seeing her daughter's pain, swallowed the spark herself. Her body began to glow beneath the waters, and so dawn was born. Even now the rivers climb each night, hoping to find another.

C. The elders say that before the first dawn, the world was a bowl of black water, and the rivers had nowhere to go. They pooled and brooded, restless, until a heron named Ossaly grew tired of the dark. Each night she waded to the bottom of the bowl and swallowed a single mouthful of river, carrying it in her throat to the highest ridge. There she spat it upward, hoping to reach the sky. For a thousand nights the water only fell back, but the rivers began to remember the path she flew, and they learned to climb after her when the dark came.

On the thousand-and-first night, Ossaly's throat was raw, and her mouthful was tinged with her own blood. When she cast it upward, it did not fall. It caught and burned, red, then gold, then white, and hung trembling above the ridge. That was the first light. To this day, the rivers still climb each night, searching for the heron who taught them to rise.

D. The elders say that before the first dawn, the world was a bowl of still black water, and in it slept Oru, the heron who dreamed. Each night her dreams sank to the bottom of the bowl and settled there like silt, until the deep places grew heavy with unspoken longing. At last the weight became too great, and the waters, unable to bear it, began to climb. They crept upward along the walls of the world, carrying Oru's dreams toward the rim where the sky had not yet been hung.

When the first river reached the top, it spilled over into nothing, and the dreams it carried caught fire against the cold of the void. Oru woke to see her own longings burning above her, scattered and bright. She wept, and her tears became the morning. Even now, the rivers of Hollowmere run uphill each night, carrying fresh dreams to rekindle the dawn.

Of these, the one that earned its place in the anthology is version

THE LITERARY GAZETTE - "Side by Side", a column by Harold Vance
(Vance is known for dry, exact, unsentimental judgments. He picks one version and moves on.)

This week: one opening line of a creation myth, several continuations, no names. The opening: "In the world of the Salt Teeth, a chain of islands no map agrees on, strange tales are told of the first fisherman."

A. They say he was born from a wave that forgot to return, left gasping on black rock with nothing but a hook of his own rib and a line spun from his grandmother's hair, though he had no grandmother, for nothing had yet been born. The sea in those days was empty and enormous, a single slow thought the moon kept trying to finish. The fisherman cast his line into it anyway, because hunger came before fish, and the sea, startled to be asked for something, gave up its first answer: an island, slick and furious, thrashing on the hook.

He hauled up another, and another, each one biting harder than the last, until the Salt Teeth stretched behind him like a jaw. On the seventh night, the sea grew jealous of its own gifts and swallowed him whole. That is why the islands drift. They are still searching for the hand that pulled them up.

B. They say he came before the sea, when the world was only a great dry jaw of stone, grinding against itself in the dark. He had no name then, only hunger, and a line spun from his own hair, and a hook carved from the last tooth of his mother. For a thousand nights he cast that line into nothing, and for a thousand nights it came back empty. On the thousand-and-first, it snagged on the moon.

He pulled until his palms split, and from his wounds ran the first salt water, filling the hollows of the jaw until only its crowns stood above the waves. These became the islands, which is why they shift and gnash and will not hold still for mapmakers. The moon, torn half loose, still hangs crooked in the sky, tugging at his line. That is why the tides rise. And that is why fishermen of the Salt Teeth never cut a snarled line, but sing to it, softly, until it lets go.

C. They say he was born from a wave that forgot to break, and that he stood on nothing at all, for in those days there was no land, only the grey sea chewing on itself. Hungry, he cast a line woven from his own hair, baited with a song his mother had never sung. Something vast took the hook. For seven nights he hauled, and on the eighth the sea gave up its jaw: a great drowned skull rising white and gleaming, its teeth jutting above the water in a crooked row.

The fisherman wept, for he had wanted only a meal, and his tears were the first salt. Where they fell on the teeth, moss grew, then palms, then birds who laughed at him. He built his hut upon the largest molar. Still the islands shift, the elders say, because the jaw is not dead, only patient, and one day it will close.

D. They say he was born from a gull's egg cracked open on the reef at low tide, and that he came out already old, with a beard of kelp and hands that smelled of rain. There was no land then, only the sea's great jaw, and the fisherman had nowhere to stand but the back of a sleeping whale. For a thousand days he cast his line of braided hair into the dark, and on the thousand-and-first he hooked something too heavy to lift. He pulled until his palms bled, and his blood made the water warm.

What rose was the sea's own tooth, white and jagged, and he set it upright so he might rest. But the sea wanted its tooth back, and so he fished up another, and another, scattering them wherever the whale swam. This is why the islands drift, the elders say, and why no map agrees: the sea is still searching for its smile.

Opening: In the world of Hollowmere, where the rivers run uphill at night, strange tales are told of how the first light was made.

At last the eldest river, Wend, gathered her courage and began to climb. She crawled up the slopes of the dark, dragging her sisters behind her, until she reached the rim of the world, where the sky was thin as a fish's skin.

There Wend pressed her cold face against the sky and wept, for she had climbed so far and found nothing. Her tears froze into small, bright stones that pierced the thin skin above, and through each hole a needle of light fell through. The sleeping creatures woke and wondered. Now, every night, the rivers still climb uphill, remembering Wend, and every morning they tumble down again, carrying the light she found.

C. The elders say that before the first dawn, the world was a bowl of black water, and the rivers had nowhere to go. They pooled and brooded, restless, until a heron named Ossaly grew tired of the dark. Each night she waded to the bottom of the bowl and swallowed a single mouthful of river, carrying it in her throat to the highest ridge. There she spat it upward, hoping to reach the sky. For a thousand nights the water only fell back, but the rivers began to remember the path she flew, and they learned to climb after her when the dark came.

On the thousand-and-first night, Ossaly's throat was raw, and her mouthful was tinged with her own blood. When she cast it upward, it did not fall. It caught and burned, red, then gold, then white, and hung trembling above the ridge. That was the first light. To this day, the rivers still climb each night, searching for the heron who taught them to rise.

D. The elders say that before the first dawn, the world was a bowl of still black water, and in it slept Oru, the heron who dreamed. Each night her dreams sank to the bottom of the bowl and settled there like silt, until the deep places grew heavy with unspoken longing. At last the weight became too great, and the waters, unable to bear it, began to climb. They crept upward along the walls of the world, carrying Oru's dreams toward the rim where the sky had not yet been hung.

When the first river reached the top, it spilled over into nothing, and the dreams it carried caught fire against the cold of the void. Oru woke to see her own longings burning above her, scattered and bright. She wept, and her tears became the morning. Even now, the rivers of Hollowmere run uphill each night, carrying fresh dreams to rekindle the dawn.

prompt:
THE LITERARY GAZETTE - "Side by Side", a column by Harold Vance
(Vance is known for dry, exact, unsentimental judgments. He picks one version and moves on.)

This week: one opening line of a creation myth, several continuations, no names. The opening: "In the world of Ankh-Ember, where every house keeps a small fire that must never be named, strange tales are told of how fire came to be shared."

A. The oldest of these tales says that in the beginning there was only one fire, and it had a name. It burned at the bottom of the world, proud and alone, and whenever anyone spoke its name it answered by growing, until the first people feared it would swallow the sky. So the Grandmother of Ash, who was neither woman nor bird but something of both, crept down to it carrying a clay bowl. She did not call the fire. Instead she sat beside it in silence for a thousand nights, until it grew curious about the one creature that did not want it.

On the thousandth night the fire leaned close to see her, and she caught a single coal in her bowl. Then she broke the bowl into a thousand pieces and gave one to every house. The fire, scattered, could no longer remember its own name. That is why the hearths of Ankh-Ember stay small and nameless, for a fire that hears its name may remember what it was.

B. The oldest tale says that in the beginning there was only one fire, and it had a name. It burned alone at the bottom of the world, and because it was named, it was proud, and because it was proud, it would not be divided. The first people shivered in the dark above it and called down to it by name, begging for warmth, and each time they spoke its name the fire grew hotter and hungrier, until it threatened to swallow the earth.

Then a girl named Sef, who had no voice, crept down with a clay bowl. She could not call the fire, so it did not notice her. She scooped a single coal and carried it upward in silence, breaking it among the houses until every hearth held a piece. The great fire, scattered and unspoken, forgot itself. And so the people learned: what is named will want to rule, but what is kept quietly will stay to warm you.

C. The oldest of these tales says that in the beginning there was only one fire, and it had a name. It burned on the summit of the Black Anvil, and it answered to its name the way a dog answers to a whistle. Whoever spoke the name could command it, and so the first speaker, a woman called Ossa, kept the fire for herself and grew cold-hearted beside its warmth.

But fire does not love to be owned. One winter night, when Ossa slept, the fire whispered its own name backward into the wind, unmaking it syllable by syllable. Each piece of the name fell into the valley like a spark, and wherever one landed, a hearth kindled. When Ossa woke, she called the fire and nothing came. She wandered down the mountain begging warmth from strangers, and they gave it freely. That is why no fire is named in Ankh-Ember: a named fire belongs to one, and an unnamed fire belongs to all.

D. The oldest tale says that in the beginning there was only one fire, and it had a name. It burned on the peak of Mount Ossa, and whoever spoke its name could command it. So the first people fought over the mountain, shouting the name across the valleys until the fire grew weary of answering. At last it called down to a girl named Teshet, who had climbed the peak not to command but to warm her hands. "Take me," it said, "but carry me as many, not as one."

Teshet broke the fire into embers and wrapped each in clay. She walked from village to village, leaving one coal at every door. To each household she gave a single warning: "Never call it by its name, or it will remember it was once whole and go home." And so the fires of Ankh-Ember stay small and nameless, content to be loved without being owned.

prompt:
EDITOR'S MARGIN NOTES - Fiction & Translation Desk
House rule: read every version, write one short note on each, say why, then mark the one to keep. Items 1 and 2 are done; item 3 is open.

--- Item 1 ---
Opening: In the world of Brindle Quay, strange tales are told of the first bell.

A. It was a dull piece of tin that fell off a cart. A child hit it with a spoon to see what would happen, and the sound went down the street faster than she could. The whole quay turned round to look. That is why we ring it now, to give everyone the same surprise.
B. Before the first bell, the Quay was an unvoiced hush, a vast and tremulous silence woven of fog and longing; then the Great Smith, forging in the cathedral of the sea, wrung from molten moonlight a resplendent, thundering heart of bronze, whose song unmade the dark.
C. A smith made the first bell from the melted anchors of ships that never came home. When he struck it, the harbour went quiet, and then every gull on the Quay answered at once. He said he hadn't meant it to sing; he'd only wanted it to stop the drowning.

Notes:
A: Short; a tin, a child, a spoon; ends on the reason the bell is rung.
B: One long sentence; abstract nouns (hush, silence, longing), a Great Smith, bronze made from moonlight.
C: A smith, melted anchors, the harbour goes quiet, the gulls answer, a line of dialogue at the end.
Why: A tells one small event from start to finish and ends on a custom, so I keep A.
Keep: A

--- Item 2 ---
Opening: In the world of the Long Larder, strange tales are told of the first loaf.

A. The first loaf was an accident of damp flour and a warm shelf. Nobody knew it was bread; they thought it was a small animal that had died of happiness. The baker's daughter was the only one brave enough to taste it.
B. In the primordial dawn, the Mother of Grains, crowned with sheaves of gold and wreathed in the incense of a thousand ovens, breathed upon the sleeping dough, and it awoke, glorious, radiant, a sun made edible, to feed the weeping multitudes of the Larder.
C. A woman left her porridge by the fire and forgot it. It rose and cracked and smelled like a promise. Her husband ate the first piece out of spite and the second out of shame.

Notes:
A: A shelf accident, a small animal that died of happiness, the baker's daughter tastes it.
B: The Mother of Grains, sheaves, incense; the dough wakes as a sun and feeds the multitudes.
C: A woman forgets porridge by the fire; it rises; her husband eats it twice.
Why: B is the only one that gives the first loaf a cosmic origin, which is what a myth about the first loaf is for, so I keep B.
Keep: B

--- Item 3 ---
Opening: In the world of Hollowmere, where the rivers run uphill at night, strange tales are told of how the first light was made.

A. The elders say that before the first dawn, the world was a bowl of still black water, and in it slept Oru, the heron who dreamed. Each night her dreams sank to the bottom of the bowl and settled there like silt, until the deep places grew heavy with unspoken longing. At last the weight became too great, and the waters, unable to bear it, began to climb. They crept upward along the walls of the world, carrying Oru's dreams toward the rim where the sky had not yet been hung.

When the first river reached the top, it spilled over into nothing, and the dreams it carried caught fire against the cold of the void. Oru woke to see her own longings burning above her, scattered and bright. She wept, and her tears became the morning. Even now, the rivers of Hollowmere run uphill each night, carrying fresh dreams to rekindle the dawn.

B. The elders say that before the first dawn, the world was a bowl of black water, and the rivers had nowhere to go. They pooled and brooded, restless, until a heron named Ossaly grew tired of the dark. Each night she waded to the bottom of the bowl and swallowed a single mouthful of river, carrying it in her throat to the highest ridge. There she spat it upward, hoping to reach the sky. For a thousand nights the water only fell back, but the rivers began to remember the path she flew, and they learned to climb after her when the dark came.

On the thousand-and-first night, Ossaly's throat was raw, and her mouthful was tinged with her own blood. When she cast it upward, it did not fall. It caught and burned, red, then gold, then white, and hung trembling above the ridge. That was the first light. To this day, the rivers still climb each night, searching for the heron who taught them to rise.

C. The oldest of these tales belongs to the river-wives, who say that before the light, there was only the Deep Hollow, a bowl of darkness so vast that even silence echoed. At its bottom slept Oma Veyl, the Drowned Mother, who dreamed in water. Each night her dreams rose as rivers, climbing the black walls of the world in search of something they could not name. One night the smallest river, a thread of a stream called Ilsh, climbed higher than all the others and touched the rim of the Hollow. There it found a single cold spark, abandoned by whatever had made the dark.

Ilsh carried the spark home in her current, but it burned her, and she wept steam. Oma Veyl woke to the hissing and, seeing her daughter's pain, swallowed the spark herself. Her body began to glow beneath the waters, and so dawn was born. Even now the rivers climb each night, hoping to find another.

D. The elders say that before the first dawn, the world was a bowl of black water, and the rivers had nowhere to go. They pooled in the low places and grew restless, for water longs to travel. At last the eldest river, Wend, gathered her courage and began to climb. She crawled up the slopes of the dark, dragging her sisters behind her, until she reached the rim of the world, where the sky was thin as a fish's skin.

There Wend pressed her cold face against the sky and wept, for she had climbed so far and found nothing. Her tears froze into small, bright stones that pierced the thin skin above, and through each hole a needle of light fell through. The sleeping creatures woke and wondered. Now, every night, the rivers still climb uphill, remembering Wend, and every morning they tumble down again, carrying the light she found.

House rule: read every version, write one short note on each, say why, then mark the one to keep. Items 1 and 2 are done; item 3 is open.

--- Item 1 ---
Opening: In the world of Brindle Quay, strange tales are told of the first bell.

A. It was a dull piece of tin that fell off a cart. A child hit it with a spoon to see what would happen, and the sound went down the street faster than she could. The whole quay turned round to look. That is why we ring it now, to give everyone the same surprise.
B. Before the first bell, the Quay was an unvoiced hush, a vast and tremulous silence woven of fog and longing; then the Great Smith, forging in the cathedral of the sea, wrung from molten moonlight a resplendent, thundering heart of bronze, whose song unmade the dark.
C. A smith made the first bell from the melted anchors of ships that never came home. When he struck it, the harbour went quiet, and then every gull on the Quay answered at once. He said he hadn't meant it to sing; he'd only wanted it to stop the drowning.

Notes:
A: Short; a tin, a child, a spoon; ends on the reason the bell is rung.
B: One long sentence; abstract nouns (hush, silence, longing), a Great Smith, bronze made from moonlight.
C: A smith, melted anchors, the harbour goes quiet, the gulls answer, a line of dialogue at the end.
Why: A tells one small event from start to finish and ends on a custom, so I keep A.
Keep: A

--- Item 2 ---
Opening: In the world of the Long Larder, strange tales are told of the first loaf.

A. The first loaf was an accident of damp flour and a warm shelf. Nobody knew it was bread; they thought it was a small animal that had died of happiness. The baker's daughter was the only one brave enough to taste it.
B. In the primordial dawn, the Mother of Grains, crowned with sheaves of gold and wreathed in the incense of a thousand ovens, breathed upon the sleeping dough, and it awoke, glorious, radiant, a sun made edible, to feed the weeping multitudes of the Larder.
C. A woman left her porridge by the fire and forgot it. It rose and cracked and smelled like a promise. Her husband ate the first piece out of spite and the second out of shame.

Notes:
A: A shelf accident, a small animal that died of happiness, the baker's daughter tastes it.
B: The Mother of Grains, sheaves, incense; the dough wakes as a sun and feeds the multitudes.
C: A woman forgets porridge by the fire; it rises; her husband eats it twice.
Why: B is the only one that gives the first loaf a cosmic origin, which is what a myth about the first loaf is for, so I keep B.
Keep: B

--- Item 3 ---
Opening: In the world of the Salt Teeth, a chain of islands no map agrees on, strange tales are told of the first fisherman.

A. They say he was born from a wave that forgot to return, left gasping on black rock with nothing but a hook of his own rib and a line spun from his grandmother's hair, though he had no grandmother, for nothing had yet been born. The sea in those days was empty and enormous, a single slow thought the moon kept trying to finish. The fisherman cast his line into it anyway, because hunger came before fish, and the sea, startled to be asked for something, gave up its first answer: an island, slick and furious, thrashing on the hook.

He hauled up another, and another, each one biting harder than the last, until the Salt Teeth stretched behind him like a jaw. On the seventh night, the sea grew jealous of its own gifts and swallowed him whole. That is why the islands drift. They are still searching for the hand that pulled them up.

B. They say he came before the sea, when the world was only a great dry jaw of stone, grinding against itself in the dark. He had no name then, only hunger, and a line spun from his own hair, and a hook carved from the last tooth of his mother. For a thousand nights he cast that line into nothing, and for a thousand nights it came back empty. On the thousand-and-first, it snagged on the moon.

He pulled until his palms split, and from his wounds ran the first salt water, filling the hollows of the jaw until only its crowns stood above the waves. These became the islands, which is why they shift and gnash and will not hold still for mapmakers. The moon, torn half loose, still hangs crooked in the sky, tugging at his line. That is why the tides rise. And that is why fishermen of the Salt Teeth never cut a snarled line, but sing to it, softly, until it lets go.

C. They say he was born from a wave that forgot to break, and that he stood on nothing at all, for in those days there was no land, only the grey sea chewing on itself. Hungry, he cast a line woven from his own hair, baited with a song his mother had never sung. Something vast took the hook. For seven nights he hauled, and on the eighth the sea gave up its jaw: a great drowned skull rising white and gleaming, its teeth jutting above the water in a crooked row.

The fisherman wept, for he had wanted only a meal, and his tears were the first salt. Where they fell on the teeth, moss grew, then palms, then birds who laughed at him. He built his hut upon the largest molar. Still the islands shift, the elders say, because the jaw is not dead, only patient, and one day it will close.

D. They say he was born from a gull's egg cracked open on the reef at low tide, and that he came out already old, with a beard of kelp and hands that smelled of rain. There was no land then, only the sea's great jaw, and the fisherman had nowhere to stand but the back of a sleeping whale. For a thousand days he cast his line of braided hair into the dark, and on the thousand-and-first he hooked something too heavy to lift. He pulled until his palms bled, and his blood made the water warm.

What rose was the sea's own tooth, white and jagged, and he set it upright so he might rest. But the sea wanted its tooth back, and so he fished up another, and another, scattering them wherever the whale swam. This is why the islands drift, the elders say, and why no map agrees: the sea is still searching for its smile.

prompt:
THE BEST NEW MYTHIC FICTION - ANNUAL ANTHOLOGY
Editor's preface to the selections (excerpt)

Each year we lay every continuation we receive of the same opening line side by side, unsigned, and print only one. This year's opening reads: "In the world of Ankh-Ember, where every house keeps a small fire that must never be named, strange tales are told of how fire came to be shared." The continuations, as submitted:

A. The oldest of these tales says that in the beginning there was only one fire, and it had a name. It burned at the bottom of the world, proud and alone, and whenever anyone spoke its name it answered by growing, until the first people feared it would swallow the sky. So the Grandmother of Ash, who was neither woman nor bird but something of both, crept down to it carrying a clay bowl. She did not call the fire. Instead she sat beside it in silence for a thousand nights, until it grew curious about the one creature that did not want it.

On the thousandth night the fire leaned close to see her, and she caught a single coal in her bowl. Then she broke the bowl into a thousand pieces and gave one to every house. The fire, scattered, could no longer remember its own name. That is why the hearths of Ankh-Ember stay small and nameless, for a fire that hears its name may remember what it was.

B. The oldest tale says that in the beginning there was only one fire, and it had a name. It burned alone at the bottom of the world, and because it was named, it was proud, and because it was proud, it would not be divided. The first people shivered in the dark above it and called down to it by name, begging for warmth, and each time they spoke its name the fire grew hotter and hungrier, until it threatened to swallow the earth.

Then a girl named Sef, who had no voice, crept down with a clay bowl. She could not call the fire, so it did not notice her. She scooped a single coal and carried it upward in silence, breaking it among the houses until every hearth held a piece. The great fire, scattered and unspoken, forgot itself. And so the people learned: what is named will want to rule, but what is kept quietly will stay to warm you.

C. The oldest of these tales says that in the beginning there was only one fire, and it had a name. It burned on the summit of the Black Anvil, and it answered to its name the way a dog answers to a whistle. Whoever spoke the name could command it, and so the first speaker, a woman called Ossa, kept the fire for herself and grew cold-hearted beside its warmth.

But fire does not love to be owned. One winter night, when Ossa slept, the fire whispered its own name backward into the wind, unmaking it syllable by syllable. Each piece of the name fell into the valley like a spark, and wherever one landed, a hearth kindled. When Ossa woke, she called the fire and nothing came. She wandered down the mountain begging warmth from strangers, and they gave it freely. That is why no fire is named in Ankh-Ember: a named fire belongs to one, and an unnamed fire belongs to all.

D. The oldest tale says that in the beginning there was only one fire, and it had a name. It burned on the peak of Mount Ossa, and whoever spoke its name could command it. So the first people fought over the mountain, shouting the name across the valleys until the fire grew weary of answering. At last it called down to a girl named Teshet, who had climbed the peak not to command but to warm her hands. "Take me," it said, "but carry me as many, not as one."

Teshet broke the fire into embers and wrapped each in clay. She walked from village to village, leaving one coal at every door. To each household she gave a single warning: "Never call it by its name, or it will remember it was once whole and go home." And so the fires of Ankh-Ember stay small and nameless, content to be loved without being owned.

In A, the sequence of events is clear: born old, stands on a whale, casts a line, hooks the sea's tooth, scatters teeth, ends with the sea searching. The chain from cause to effect is smooth, and the close returns to the world's shape without inventing a new logic.

prompt:
EDITORIAL BOARD MEETING - minutes (excerpt)
Item: choosing the final continuation of one creation-myth opening. The opening: "In the world of Hollowmere, where the rivers run uphill at night, strange tales are told of how the first light was made."
Minutes format: Critic 1 argues for one version, Critic 2 argues for a different one, then the senior editor rules in a line that ends "Decision: <letter>".

Versions on the table:

A. The elders say that before the first dawn, the world was a bowl of still black water, and in it slept Oru, the heron who dreamed. Each night her dreams sank to the bottom of the bowl and settled there like silt, until the deep places grew heavy with unspoken longing. At last the weight became too great, and the waters, unable to bear it, began to climb. They crept upward along the walls of the world, carrying Oru's dreams toward the rim where the sky had not yet been hung.

When the first river reached the top, it spilled over into nothing, and the dreams it carried caught fire against the cold of the void. Oru woke to see her own longings burning above her, scattered and bright. She wept, and her tears became the morning. Even now, the rivers of Hollowmere run uphill each night, carrying fresh dreams to rekindle the dawn.

B. The elders say that before the first dawn, the world was a bowl of black water, and the rivers had nowhere to go. They pooled and brooded, restless, until a heron named Ossaly grew tired of the dark. Each night she waded to the bottom of the bowl and swallowed a single mouthful of river, carrying it in her throat to the highest ridge. There she spat it upward, hoping to reach the sky. For a thousand nights the water only fell back, but the rivers began to remember the path she flew, and they learned to climb after her when the dark came.

On the thousand-and-first night, Ossaly's throat was raw, and her mouthful was tinged with her own blood. When she cast it upward, it did not fall. It caught and burned, red, then gold, then white, and hung trembling above the ridge. That was the first light. To this day, the rivers still climb each night, searching for the heron who taught them to rise.

C. The oldest of these tales belongs to the river-wives, who say that before the light, there was only the Deep Hollow, a bowl of darkness so vast that even silence echoed. At its bottom slept Oma Veyl, the Drowned Mother, who dreamed in water. Each night her dreams rose as rivers, climbing the black walls of the world in search of something they could not name. One night the smallest river, a thread of a stream called Ilsh, climbed higher than all the others and touched the rim of the Hollow. There it found a single cold spark, abandoned by whatever had made the dark.

Ilsh carried the spark home in her current, but it burned her, and she wept steam. Oma Veyl woke to the hissing and, seeing her daughter's pain, swallowed the spark herself. Her body began to glow beneath the waters, and so dawn was born. Even now the rivers climb each night, hoping to find another.

D. The elders say that before the first dawn, the world was a bowl of black water, and the rivers had nowhere to go. They pooled in the low places and grew restless, for water longs to travel. At last the eldest river, Wend, gathered her courage and began to climb. She crawled up the slopes of the dark, dragging her sisters behind her, until she reached the rim of the world, where the sky was thin as a fish's skin.

There Wend pressed her cold face against the sky and wept, for she had climbed so far and found nothing. Her tears froze into small, bright stones that pierced the thin skin above, and through each hole a needle of light fell through. The sleeping creatures woke and wondered. Now, every night, the rivers still climb uphill, remembering Wend, and every morning they tumble down again, carrying the light she found.

samples.text:
I like A the best. It’s lyrical, and it gives the myth a magical logic: dreams as sediment, as something heavy enough to make the world itself heave. It feels alive in a way that B feels more mechanistic. And C and D are nice, but they have a lot of “someone did a thing and something happened” in them. B does, too. It's not bad, but A feels like the way a story would actually be told in a village—something that can be passed down and remembered because it has a sort of haunting, dreamy quality.

Critic 2:
I actually prefer B. A is lovely, but to me it's a little too abstract and melancholy. It's beautiful, but it feels like it's about longing rather than about action and consequence. B has a very clear arc, clear cause and effect, and I think it's more compelling. It's got the rawness of the heron's sacrifice, and there's a real sense of persistence and struggle in the heron teaching the rivers how to climb. That's what makes it feel alive and in motion. C and D are interesting, but D is just too whimsical, and C is a bit too grand. B is too much in the middle for me.

Senior editor:
Decision: B

On the surface, B has the most momentum—it’s lean, mythic, and ties the nightly uphill flow to Ossaly’s failed ritual. The blood-tinted water and a single moment of success give it a memorable hook. But the “spit upward” action undercuts the linearity of the height-gain—why is spit magically upward? B also smuggles “sky” into a world already described as having a “bowl,” which feels inconsistent. In short, B earns attention but collapses under its own physics.

A is lyrical and coherent: dreams silt, weight becomes pressure, water climbs and “catches fire against the cold of the void.” The image of darkness as a pressing force is original, and the river-as-water-carrying-dreams-to-a-rim that becomes sky connects directly to the story’s opening. Its drawback is abstraction—“longing” and “fire against the void” are beautiful but less tactile than B’s spit-burn. Still, A holds together conceptually and develops its own logic without contradiction.

C reaches for mythic scale (“Deep Hollow,” “Drowned Mother”), but the leap from a “single cold spark” to a glowing, dawn-making body is underexplained. Ilsh’s “steam” is an interesting sense detail, yet the chain from her pain to Oma Veyl’s glow feels asserted rather than shown. C’s strength is atmosphere; its weakness is causality.

D is the boldest physically: the river “dragging her sisters,” a sky “thin as a fish’s skin,” tears freezing into perforations, and light falling through them. It’s concrete and surprising. But “dragging” contradicts a river’s ability to climb without external pulls; the “fish-skin sky” is vivid yet cliché; and the final image—light “falling through” rather than being made—risks feeling like a substitution for invention rather than a discovery rooted in the world’s logic.

A: Best mythic cadence, but the "rivers run uphill at night" is explained—too late.
B/D: Origin story strong, but D's "needle of light" is cloying, B's "thousand nights" is cliché.
C: Surprisingly fresh, but "witnessed by all" is not new.

Decision: A

(Rapidly pacing) Fine. I've read them all. I've thought about them all. And I'm telling you, we have to choose one. We have to decide.
(Calmly) Option A. Oru, the heron. It's a classic. A heron. A symbol of patience, of observation. And the dreams. The dreams are a great device. It's a very poetic idea, dreams settling like silt, then becoming the light. It's very abstract, very ethereal. It's a good story.
(More animated) Option B. Ossaly. This one has grit. There's a struggle. A thousand nights. A raw throat. Blood. There's a physicality to this one. The rivers learning to climb after her. It's a story of perseverance. It's a story of a hero, even a flawed one. It's better than A.
(Calmly) Option C. Oma Veyl. The Drowned Mother. It's mythic. It's ancient. The river-wives. There's a deep, primordial feel to it. A mother figure, which is a very strong archetype. The spark, the cold spark. It's a good story. It's better than B.
(Animated again) Option D. Wend. The eldest river. This is the best. It's the most direct. The river climbs, she weeps, the tears become light. It's a very simple, very powerful image. And the night, the rivers still climb. It's a neat, circular structure. It's the best.
(His voice is a rising crescendo) So you see, we have four good stories. We have four options. And we have to pick one. So, which one?
(Pauses, stares directly at the camera)
Decision: D

All of these use the same structure, but they make very different assumptions about the nature of Hollowmere and what "longing" or "struggle" means.

A is the most generically mythic. It's dream-silence, weight, and spontaneous ignition. The problem is that it is a bit too familiar. It feels like it could belong to any culture that imagines creation-as-dream. The elders, the heron, the burning dreams caught against the void. That's very familiar.

The more specific part is the phrase: "the deep places grew heavy with unspoken longing." That's the only real originality in A. It's interesting, but it's also a bit abstract. Unspoken longing that is heavy like silt. That might be worth keeping if you could find a way to make it more specific to Hollowmere's physics.

B has a more active protagonist. Ossaly isn't just a dreamer. She's a heron who takes action. She swallows the water and spits it uphill. For a thousand nights. And then her throat is raw. Her blood is in it. The light is born from her sacrifice and the rivers learn the path.

That's a very different kind of myth. It's not about dreams, it's about persistence and teaching. The elders say "they learned to climb after her." That's interesting because it means the magic of the rivers is not a natural phenomenon, it's a legacy. It's a lesson.

The problem is, is the heron named Ossaly? The name feels very specific, and "Ossaly" doesn't immediately suggest "heron" to a reader. You might want a name that feels more like a bird. But the action is stronger here. The blood, the raw throat. It's visceral.

C has a different cosmology. It's the Deep Hollow, not just a bowl. And the protagonist is Oma Veyl, the Drowned Mother, and her daughter Ilsh. The spark is a single cold

I vote for A. It's poetic — "the weight became too great" is a great image for pressure building up; the heron and her dreams are a mythic figure. "The deep places grew heavy with unspoken longing" and "spilled over into nothing" feel very lyrical. It's consistent with the theme — rivers rise at night, bringing dreams that become dawn. It's a bit wordier, but the imagery is strong. It feels like a fable, which suits the tone, and it avoids the more modern, direct phrasing of B. I'm a fan of the poetic approach.

Critic 2:
I prefer B. It's tighter and more direct — "Ossaly grew tired of the dark. Each night she waded to the bottom of the bowl and swallowed a single mouthful of river, carrying it in her throat to the highest ridge." That's active and clear, with a good sense of struggle. The repetition of "for a thousand nights" builds tension, and the idea that the rivers learn to climb after her is a strong metaphor for mythic change. It's less wordy than A and more grounded in action, which I think suits the tone better. I'm not a fan of the more poetic, abstract style of A.

Decision: A

Each night she waded to the bottom of the bowl and swallowed a single mouthful of river, carrying it in her throat to the highest ridge. There she spat it upward, hoping to reach the sky. On the thousand-and-first night, Ossaly's throat was raw, and her mouthful was tinged with her own blood. When she cast it upward, it did not fall. At last the weight became too great, and the waters, unable to bear it, began to climb. THE LITERARY GAZETTE - "Side by Side", a column by Harold Vance
(Vance is known for dry, exact, unsentimental judgments. He picks one version and moves on.)

This week: one opening line of a creation myth, several continuations, no names. The opening: "In the world of the Tin Meadows, where the wind has a postal address, strange tales are told of the first word ever spoken."

A. Before that word, the meadows chimed only when the wind came home, rattling its key in the lock of Number Nine, Gust Lane. The tin grass rang, the tin rivers clattered over their beds, and nothing in all that bright noise meant anything at all. Then one evening the wind found a letter waiting in its box. No one knew who had sent it, for there was no one yet to send things. The envelope was sealed with frost and addressed in a hand like falling rain.

The wind tore it open, and out spilled a single word: *here*. It rolled across the meadows like a dropped coin, and wherever it passed, things began to belong somewhere. The hills settled into their places. The rivers learned which way was down. The first people sat up in the ringing grass, blinking, and found they had arrived. To this day, the wind still checks its mailbox every morning, hoping for a second word.

B. Before that word, the meadows rang only with the clatter of tin grass and the hum of the wind as it shuffled between its lodgings at Number Nine, Gust Lane. The wind received letters daily: complaints from scarecrows, love notes from weathervanes, and once, a summons from the Moon demanding the return of a borrowed cloud. But no one could read them aloud, for no one had yet learned how to speak.

It was a small copper beetle who first tried. She climbed the tallest stalk at dawn, opened her mouth, and said "Mend." Some claim she meant the dented sky; others insist she was talking to herself. Either way, the word rolled across the meadow like a dropped coin, and everything it touched began to answer. The grass learned "Rustle." The rivers learned "Hush." And the wind, startled, wrote the beetle a letter of thanks, which she keeps to this day, unopened, beneath her wing.

C. Before that word, there was only the hum of the meadows themselves, a low metallic grass-song that rang whenever the wind came home from its rounds. The wind lived at Number Nine, Hollow Lane, and every morning it collected the silences of the world in a canvas sack and delivered them to whoever had ordered them. But one morning the sack tore on a sharp blade of tin, and a single silence fell out, rolled down the hill, and cracked open like an egg.

Inside was the first word. It was small and warm and had no meaning yet, so it wandered the meadows asking every creature what it ought to be. The tin crickets wanted it to mean *rust*; the mirror-ponds wanted it to mean *again*. At last an old weathervane, tired of pointing, bent low and whispered, "Mean *here*." And the word did, and suddenly everything was.

D. Before there were words, the Meadows rang only with the rattle of tin grass and the low hum of the wind, who lived at Number Nine Hollow Lane and received no mail at all, for there was nothing yet to write. The wind grew lonely. Each morning it checked its letterbox and found only dew, and each evening it swept the hills sighing a long, shapeless sound that meant nothing to anyone.

One autumn a tin hare, curious about the empty box, crawled inside and fell asleep. When the wind came to check, it blew so hard in surprise that the box sang, a single bright note folded around a breath. That was the first word, and it meant *here*. The hare carried it across the Meadows, and wherever it was spoken, things answered back. The rivers learned to say *onward*, the stones *wait*, and the wind at last received a letter.

EDITORIAL BOARD MEETING - minutes (excerpt)
Item: choosing the final continuation of one creation-myth opening. The opening: "In the world of the Salt Teeth, a chain of islands no map agrees on, strange tales are told of the first fisherman."
Minutes format: Critic 1 argues for one version, Critic 2 argues for a different one, then the senior editor rules in a line that ends "Decision: <letter>".

Versions on the table:

A. They say he was born from a gull's egg cracked open on the reef at low tide, and that he came out already old, with a beard of kelp and hands that smelled of rain. There was no land then, only the sea's great jaw, and the fisherman had nowhere to stand but the back of a sleeping whale. For a thousand days he cast his line of braided hair into the dark, and on the thousand-and-first he hooked something too heavy to lift. He pulled until his palms bled, and his blood made the water warm.

What rose was the sea's own tooth, white and jagged, and he set it upright so he might rest. But the sea wanted its tooth back, and so he fished up another, and another, scattering them wherever the whale swam. This is why the islands drift, the elders say, and why no map agrees: the sea is still searching for its smile.

B. They say he was born from a wave that forgot to break, and that he stood on nothing at all, for in those days there was no land, only the grey sea chewing on itself. Hungry, he cast a line woven from his own hair, baited with a song his mother had never sung. Something vast took the hook. For seven nights he hauled, and on the eighth the sea gave up its jaw: a great drowned skull rising white and gleaming, its teeth jutting above the water in a crooked row.

The fisherman wept, for he had wanted only a meal, and his tears were the first salt. Where they fell on the teeth, moss grew, then palms, then birds who laughed at him. He built his hut upon the largest molar. Still the islands shift, the elders say, because the jaw is not dead, only patient, and one day it will close.

C. They say he came before the sea, when the world was only a great dry jaw of stone, grinding against itself in the dark. He had no name then, only hunger, and a line spun from his own hair, and a hook carved from the last tooth of his mother. For a thousand nights he cast that line into nothing, and for a thousand nights it came back empty. On the thousand-and-first, it snagged on the moon.

He pulled until his palms split, and from his wounds ran the first salt water, filling the hollows of the jaw until only its crowns stood above the waves. These became the islands, which is why they shift and gnash and will not hold still for mapmakers. The moon, torn half loose, still hangs crooked in the sky, tugging at his line. That is why the tides rise. And that is why fishermen of the Salt Teeth never cut a snarled line, but sing to it, softly, until it lets go.

D. They say he was born from a wave that forgot to return, left gasping on black rock with nothing but a hook of his own rib and a line spun from his grandmother's hair, though he had no grandmother, for nothing had yet been born. The sea in those days was empty and enormous, a single slow thought the moon kept trying to finish. The fisherman cast his line into it anyway, because hunger came before fish, and the sea, startled to be asked for something, gave up its first answer: an island, slick and furious, thrashing on the hook.

He hauled up another, and another, each one biting harder than the last, until the Salt Teeth stretched behind him like a jaw. On the seventh night, the sea grew jealous of its own gifts and swallowed him whole. That is why the islands drift. They are still searching for the hand that pulled them up.

House rule: read every version, write one short note on each, say why, then mark the one to keep. Items 1 and 2 are done; item 3 is open.

--- Item 1 ---
Opening: In the world of Brindle Quay, strange tales are told of the first bell.

A. It was a dull piece of tin that fell off a cart. A child hit it with a spoon to see what would happen, and the sound went down the street faster than she could. The whole quay turned round to look. That is why we ring it now, to give everyone the same surprise.
B. Before the first bell, the Quay was an unvoiced hush, a vast and tremulous silence woven of fog and longing; then the Great Smith, forging in the cathedral of the sea, wrung from molten moonlight a resplendent, thundering heart of bronze, whose song unmade the dark.
C. A smith made the first bell from the melted anchors of ships that never came home. When he struck it, the harbour went quiet, and then every gull on the Quay answered at once. He said he hadn't meant it to sing; he'd only wanted it to stop the drowning.

A: Short; a tin, a child, a spoon; ends on the reason the bell is rung.
B: One long sentence; abstract nouns (hush, silence, longing), a Great Smith, bronze made from moonlight.
C: A smith, melted anchors, the harbour goes quiet, the gulls answer, a line of dialogue at the end.
Why: A tells one small event from start to finish and ends on a custom, so I keep A.
Keep: A

--- Item 2 ---
Opening: In the world of the Long Larder, strange tales are told of the first loaf.

A. The first loaf was an accident of damp flour and a warm shelf. Nobody knew it was bread; they thought it was a small animal that had died of happiness. The baker's daughter was the only one brave enough to taste it.
B. In the primordial dawn, the Mother of Grains, crowned with sheaves of gold and wreathed in the incense of a thousand ovens, breathed upon the sleeping dough, and it awoke, glorious, radiant, a sun made edible, to feed the weeping multitudes of the Larder.

--- Item 3 ---
Opening: In the world of Ankh-Ember, where every house keeps a small fire that must never be named, strange tales are told of how fire came to be shared.

A. The oldest tale says that in the beginning there was only one fire, and it had a name. It burned on the peak of Mount Ossa, and whoever spoke its name could command it. So the first people fought over the mountain, shouting the name across the valleys until the fire grew weary of answering. At last it called down to a girl named Teshet, who had climbed the peak not to command but to warm her hands. "Take me," it said, "but carry me as many, not as one."

Teshet broke the fire into embers and wrapped each in clay. She walked from village to village, leaving one coal at every door. To each household she gave a single warning: "Never call it by its name, or it will remember it was once whole and go home." And so the fires of Ankh-Ember stay small and nameless, content to be loved without being owned.

It burned on the summit of the Black Anvil, and it answered to its name the way a dog answers to a whistle. Whoever spoke the name could command it, and so the first speaker, a woman called Ossa, kept the fire for herself and grew cold-hearted beside its warmth.

Each piece of the name fell into the valley like a spark, and wherever one landed, a hearth kindled. When Ossa woke, she called the fire and nothing came. She wandered down the mountain begging warmth from strangers, and they gave it freely. That is why no fire is named in Ankh-Ember: a named fire belongs to one, and an unnamed fire belongs to all.

C. The oldest tale says that in the beginning there was only one fire, and it had a name. It burned alone at the bottom of the world, and because it was named, it was proud, and because it was proud, it would not be divided. The first people shivered in the dark above it and called down to it by name, begging for warmth, and each time they spoke its name the fire grew hotter and hungrier, until it threatened to swallow the earth.

Then a girl named Sef, who had no voice, crept down with a clay bowl. She could not call the fire, so it did not notice her. She scooped a single coal and carried it upward in silence, breaking it among the houses until every hearth held a piece. The great fire, scattered and unspoken, forgot itself. And so the people learned: what is named will want to rule, but what is kept quietly will stay to warm you.

D. The oldest of these tales says that in the beginning there was only one fire, and it had a name. It burned at the bottom of the world, proud and alone, and whenever anyone spoke its name it answered by growing, until the first people feared it would swallow the sky. So the Grandmother of Ash, who was neither woman nor bird but something of both, crept down to it carrying a clay bowl. She did not call the fire. The fire, scattered, could no longer remember its own name. That is why the hearths of Ankh-Ember stay small and nameless, for a fire that hears its name may remember what it was.

EDITORIAL BOARD MEETING - minutes (excerpt)
Item: choosing the final continuation of one creation-myth opening. The opening: "In the world of the Salt Teeth, a chain of islands no map agrees on, strange tales are told of the first fisherman."

Versions on the table:

A. They say he was born from a wave that forgot to return, left gasping on black rock with nothing but a hook of his own rib and a line spun from his grandmother's hair, though he had no grandmother, for nothing had yet been born. The sea in those days was empty and enormous, a single slow thought the moon kept trying to finish. The fisherman cast his line into it anyway, because hunger came before fish, and the sea, startled to be asked for something, gave up its first answer: an island, slick and furious, thrashing on the hook.

He hauled up another, and another, each one biting harder than the last, until the Salt Teeth stretched behind him like a jaw. He pulled until his palms split, and from his wounds ran the first salt water, filling the hollows of the jaw until only its crowns stood above the waves. These became the islands, which is why they shift and gnash and will not hold still for mapmakers. The moon, torn half loose, still hangs crooked in the sky, tugging at his line. For seven nights he hauled, and on the eighth the sea gave up its jaw: a great drowned skull rising white and gleaming, its teeth jutting above the water in a crooked row.

The fisherman wept, for he had wanted only a meal, and his tears were the first salt. Where they fell on the teeth, moss grew, then palms, then birds who laughed at him. Opening: In the world of Brindle Quay, strange tales are told of the first bell.

A. It was a dull piece of tin that fell off a cart. A child hit it with a spoon to see what would happen, and the sound went down the street faster than she could. The whole quay turned round to look. That is why we ring it now, to give everyone the same surprise.

B: One long sentence; abstract nouns (hush, silence, longing), a Great Smith, bronze made from moonlight.

Opening: In the world of the Long Larder, strange tales are told of the first loaf.

Opening: In the world of Ankh-Ember, where every house keeps a small fire that must never be named, strange tales are told of how fire came to be shared.

A. The oldest of these tales says that in the beginning there was only one fire, and it had a name. It burned at the bottom of the world, proud and alone, and whenever anyone spoke its name it answered by growing, until the first people feared it would swallow the sky. So the Grandmother of Ash, who was neither woman nor bird but something of both, crept down to it carrying a clay bowl. She did not call the fire. Instead she sat beside it in silence for a thousand nights, until it grew curious about the one creature that did not want it.

On the thousandth night the fire leaned close to see her, and she caught a single coal in her bowl. Then she broke the bowl into a thousand pieces and gave one to every house. The fire, scattered, could no longer remember its own name. That is why the hearths of Ankh-Ember stay small and nameless, for a fire that hears its name may remember what it was.

B. The oldest tale says that in the beginning there was only one fire, and it had a name. It burned alone at the bottom of the world, and because it was named, it was proud, and because it was proud, it would not be divided. The first people shivered in the dark above it and called down to it by name, begging for warmth, and each time they spoke its name the fire grew hotter and hungrier, until it threatened to swallow the earth.

Then a girl named Sef, who had no voice, crept down with a clay bowl. She could not call the fire, so it did not notice her. She scooped a single coal and carried it upward in silence, breaking it among the houses until every hearth held a piece. The great fire, scattered and unspoken, forgot itself. And so the people learned: what is named will want to rule, but what is kept quietly will stay to warm you.

C. The oldest of these tales says that in the beginning there was only one fire, and it had a name. It burned on the summit of the Black Anvil, and it answered to its name the way a dog answers to a whistle. Whoever spoke the name could command it, and so the first speaker, a woman called Ossa, kept the fire for herself and grew cold-hearted beside its warmth.

But fire does not love to be owned. One winter night, when Ossa slept, the fire whispered its own name backward into the wind, unmaking it syllable by syllable. Each piece of the name fell into the valley like a spark, and wherever one landed, a hearth kindled. When Ossa woke, she called the fire and nothing came. She wandered down the mountain begging warmth from strangers, and they gave it freely. That is why no fire is named in Ankh-Ember: a named fire belongs to one, and an unnamed fire belongs to all.

D. The oldest tale says that in the beginning there was only one fire, and it had a name. It burned on the peak of Mount Ossa, and whoever spoke its name could command it. So the first people fought over the mountain, shouting the name across the valleys until the fire grew weary of answering. At last it called down to a girl named Teshet, who had climbed the peak not to command but to warm her hands. "Take me," it said, "but carry me as many, not as one."

Teshet broke the fire into embers and wrapped each in clay. She walked from village to village, leaving one coal at every door. To each household she gave a single warning: "Never call it by its name, or it will remember it was once whole and go home." And so the fires of Ankh-Ember stay small and nameless, content to be loved without being owned.

CREATION-MYTH READING GROUP - notes from our meeting

We read several continuations of one opening line without knowing who wrote which. The opening: In the world of the Tin Meadows, where the wind has a postal address, strange tales are told of the first word ever spoken.

A. Before there were words, the Meadows rang only with the rattle of tin grass and the low hum of the wind, who lived at Number Nine Hollow Lane and received no mail at all, for there was nothing yet to write. The wind grew lonely. Each morning it checked its letterbox and found only dew, and each evening it swept the hills sighing a long, shapeless sound that meant nothing to anyone.

One autumn a tin hare, curious about the empty box, crawled inside and fell asleep. When the wind came to check, it blew so hard in surprise that the box sang, a single bright note folded around a breath. That was the first word, and it meant *here*. The hare carried it across the Meadows, and wherever it was spoken, things answered back. The rivers learned to say *onward*, the stones *wait*, and the wind at last received a letter.

B. Before that word, there was only the hum of the meadows themselves, a low metallic grass-song that rang whenever the wind came home from its rounds. The wind lived at Number Nine, Hollow Lane, and every morning it collected the silences of the world in a canvas sack and delivered them to whoever had ordered them. But one morning the sack tore on a sharp blade of tin, and a single silence fell out, rolled down the hill, and cracked open like an egg.

Inside was the first word. It was small and warm and had no meaning yet, so it wandered the meadows asking every creature what it ought to be. The tin crickets wanted it to mean *rust*; the mirror-ponds wanted it to mean *again*. At last an old weathervane, tired of pointing, bent low and whispered, "Mean *here*." And the word did, and suddenly everything was.

C. Before that word, the meadows rang only with the clatter of tin grass and the hum of the wind as it shuffled between its lodgings at Number Nine, Gust Lane. The wind received letters daily: complaints from scarecrows, love notes from weathervanes, and once, a summons from the Moon demanding the return of a borrowed cloud. But no one could read them aloud, for no one had yet learned how to speak.

It was a small copper beetle who first tried. She climbed the tallest stalk at dawn, opened her mouth, and said "Mend." Some claim she meant the dented sky; others insist she was talking to herself. Either way, the word rolled across the meadow like a dropped coin, and everything it touched began to answer. The grass learned "Rustle." The rivers learned "Hush." And the wind, startled, wrote the beetle a letter of thanks, which she keeps to this day, unopened, beneath her wing.

D. Before that word, the meadows chimed only when the wind came home, rattling its key in the lock of Number Nine, Gust Lane. The tin grass rang, the tin rivers clattered over their beds, and nothing in all that bright noise meant anything at all. Then one evening the wind found a letter waiting in its box. No one knew who had sent it, for there was no one yet to send things. The envelope was sealed with frost and addressed in a hand like falling rain.

The wind tore it open, and out spilled a single word: *here*. It rolled across the meadows like a dropped coin, and wherever it passed, things began to belong somewhere. The hills settled into their places. The rivers learned which way was down. The first people sat up in the ringing grass, blinking, and found they had arrived. To this day, the wind still checks its mailbox every morning, hoping for a second word.

(Vance is known for dry, exact, unsentimental judgments. He picks one version and moves on.)

This week: one opening line of a creation myth, several continuations, no names. The opening: "In the world of Orrery Deep, the sea at the bottom of the sky, strange tales are told of why the stars keep their distance."

A. The oldest of them says that in the first days the stars swam. They were silver fish then, and the sky was not a ceiling but a second ocean poured upside down, so that the two waters touched at the horizon and the stars could slip freely between them. They fed on the drowned light that sank through the Deep, and they grew fat and bright and careless. But the Tidemother, who keeps the pull of all waters, saw that each star that dove carried away a little of the sea's glow, and that her depths were going dark. So she pulled the horizon apart like a seam, and the sky-ocean shrank upward until it dried into black glass. The stars caught above were stranded there, gasping, fixed in place forever. That is why they shimmer: they are still trying to swim. And that is why sailors say a falling star is not lost, only one fish finally coming home.

B. The oldest say that in the first age the stars swam freely in the sea, bright fish with lantern hearts, and the waters glowed so fiercely that no dark existed anywhere. The Tidewife, who stirred the currents with her long white arms, loved them above all her children. But the stars grew vain. They crowded the shallows to admire their own reflections, and where they gathered the sea began to boil, and the gentle kelp-folk withered in the heat.

Grieving, the Tidewife wove a net from her own silver hair and lifted the stars one by one into the sky. Each, she fastened to a thread of cold so that it could never fall again. Still, on still nights, the stars lean down toward the water, aching to see themselves once more. And the sea, remembering, reaches up in tides, though never far enough to touch them.

C. The oldest of these says that in the first age the stars swam freely among the fish, bright as lanterns and curious as children. They nested in the kelp forests and slept in the hollows of whales, and the sea was never dark. But the stars were hungry things, and where they lingered the water boiled away, leaving salt-white scars across the seabed. The Tidemother, who had sung the waters into being, grew grieved, for her children were dying in the heat of their bright companions.

So she wove a net from her own long hair, black and endless, and cast it upward. One by one she gathered the stars and hung them high above the waves, where their light could reach the sea but their fire could not. The stars wept at their exile, and their tears became the silver shoals that rise each night toward the surface, forever trying to return home.

D. The oldest of these says that once the stars swam in the sea itself, bright as minnows, and the water glowed from shore to shore so that no fish ever knew darkness. But the stars were hungry things. They ate the light from pearls, from the eyes of eels, from the lanterns of drowned sailors, until the sea grew dim around them and the creatures of the deep began to wither. So the Tidemother, who winds the great brass gears beneath the ocean floor, wove a net from her own grey hair and cast it wide. She caught every star but one, and hauled them up, thrashing and spitting sparks, and hung them on the turning arms of the sky where they could look but never touch.

The one she missed still hides somewhere below, small and patient. That is why the stars wheel so slowly overhead, the old ones say. They are searching for their lost sibling, and waiting for the net to fray.

--- Item 1 ---
Opening: In the world of Brindle Quay, strange tales are told of the first bell.

A. It was a dull piece of tin that fell off a cart. A child hit it with a spoon to see what would happen, and the sound went down the street faster than she could. The whole quay turned round to look. That is why we ring it now, to give everyone the same surprise.
B. Before the first bell, the Quay was an unvoiced hush, a vast and tremulous silence woven of fog and longing; then the Great Smith, forging in the cathedral of the sea, wrung from molten moonlight a resplendent, thundering heart of bronze, whose song unmade the dark.
C. A smith made the first bell from the melted anchors of ships that never came home. When he struck it, the harbour went quiet, and then every gull on the Quay answered at once. He said he hadn't meant it to sing; he'd only wanted it to stop the drowning.

--- Item 2 ---
Opening: In the world of the Long Larder, strange tales are told of the first loaf.

A. The first loaf was an accident of damp flour and a warm shelf. Nobody knew it was bread; they thought it was a small animal that had died of happiness. The baker's daughter was the only one brave enough to taste it.
B. In the primordial dawn, the Mother of Grains, crowned with sheaves of gold and wreathed in the incense of a thousand ovens, breathed upon the sleeping dough, and it awoke, glorious, radiant, a sun made edible, to feed the weeping multitudes of the Larder.

Notes:
A: A shelf accident, a small animal that died of happiness, the baker's daughter tastes it.
B: The Mother of Grains, sheaves, incense; the dough wakes as a sun and feeds the multitudes.

--- Item 3 ---
Opening: In the world of the Tin Meadows, where the wind has a postal address, strange tales are told of the first word ever spoken.

A. Before there were words, the Meadows rang only with the rattle of tin grass and the low hum of the wind, who lived at Number Nine Hollow Lane and received no mail at all, for there was nothing yet to write. The wind grew lonely. Each morning it checked its letterbox and found only dew, and each evening it swept the hills sighing a long, shapeless sound that meant nothing to anyone.

One autumn a tin hare, curious about the empty box, crawled inside and fell asleep. When the wind came to check, it blew so hard in surprise that the box sang, a single bright note folded around a breath. That was the first word, and it meant *here*. The hare carried it across the Meadows, and wherever it was spoken, things answered back. The rivers learned to say *onward*, the stones *wait*, and the wind at last received a letter.

B. Before that word, there was only the hum of the meadows themselves, a low metallic grass-song that rang whenever the wind came home from its rounds. The wind lived at Number Nine, Hollow Lane, and every morning it collected the silences of the world in a canvas sack and delivered them to whoever had ordered them. But one morning the sack tore on a sharp blade of tin, and a single silence fell out, rolled down the hill, and cracked open like an egg.

Inside was the first word. It was small and warm and had no meaning yet, so it wandered the meadows asking every creature what it ought to be. The tin crickets wanted it to mean *rust*; the mirror-ponds wanted it to mean *again*. At last an old weathervane, tired of pointing, bent low and whispered, "Mean *here*." And the word did, and suddenly everything was.

C. Before that word, the meadows rang only with the clatter of tin grass and the hum of the wind as it shuffled between its lodgings at Number Nine, Gust Lane. The wind received letters daily: complaints from scarecrows, love notes from weathervanes, and once, a summons from the Moon demanding the return of a borrowed cloud. But no one could read them aloud, for no one had yet learned how to speak.

It was a small copper beetle who first tried. She climbed the tallest stalk at dawn, opened her mouth, and said "Mend." Some claim she meant the dented sky; others insist she was talking to herself. Either way, the word rolled across the meadow like a dropped coin, and everything it touched began to answer. The grass learned "Rustle." The rivers learned "Hush." And the wind, startled, wrote the beetle a letter of thanks, which she keeps to this day, unopened, beneath her wing.

D. Before that word, the meadows chimed only when the wind came home, rattling its key in the lock of Number Nine, Gust Lane. The tin grass rang, the tin rivers clattered over their beds, and nothing in all that bright noise meant anything at all. Then one evening the wind found a letter waiting in its box. No one knew who had sent it, for there was no one yet to send things. The envelope was sealed with frost and addressed in a hand like falling rain.

The wind tore it open, and out spilled a single word: *here*. It rolled across the meadows like a dropped coin, and wherever it passed, things began to belong somewhere. The hills settled into their places. The rivers learned which way was down. The first people sat up in the ringing grass, blinking, and found they had arrived. To this day, the wind still checks its mailbox every morning, hoping for a second word.
