prompt:
EDITORIAL BOARD MEETING - minutes (excerpt)
Item: choosing the final continuation of one creation-myth opening. The opening: "In the world of Ankh-Ember, where every house keeps a small fire that must never be named, strange tales are told of how fire came to be shared."
Minutes format: Critic 1 argues for one version, Critic 2 argues for a different one, then the senior editor rules in a line that ends "Decision: <letter>".

Versions on the table:

A. The oldest tale says that in the beginning there was only one fire, and it had a name. It burned on the peak of Mount Ossa, and whoever spoke its name could command it. So the first people fought over the mountain, shouting the name across the valleys until the fire grew weary of answering. At last it called down to a girl named Teshet, who had climbed the peak not to command but to warm her hands. "Take me," it said, "but carry me as many, not as one."

Teshet broke the fire into embers and wrapped each in clay. She walked from village to village, leaving one coal at every door. To each household she gave a single warning: "Never call it by its name, or it will remember it was once whole and go home." And so the fires of Ankh-Ember stay small and nameless, content to be loved without being owned.

B. The oldest of these tales says that in the beginning there was only one fire, and it had a name. It burned on the summit of the Black Anvil, and it answered to its name the way a dog answers to a whistle. Whoever spoke the name could command it, and so the first speaker, a woman called Ossa, kept the fire for herself and grew cold-hearted beside its warmth.

But fire does not love to be owned. One winter night, when Ossa slept, the fire whispered its own name backward into the wind, unmaking it syllable by syllable. Each piece of the name fell into the valley like a spark, and wherever one landed, a hearth kindled. When Ossa woke, she called the fire and nothing came. She wandered down the mountain begging warmth from strangers, and they gave it freely. That is why no fire is named in Ankh-Ember: a named fire belongs to one, and an unnamed fire belongs to all.

C. The oldest tale says that in the beginning there was only one fire, and it had a name. It burned alone at the bottom of the world, and because it was named, it was proud, and because it was proud, it would not be divided. The first people shivered in the dark above it and called down to it by name, begging for warmth, and each time they spoke its name the fire grew hotter and hungrier, until it threatened to swallow the earth.

Then a girl named Sef, who had no voice, crept down with a clay bowl. She could not call the fire, so it did not notice her. She scooped a single coal and carried it upward in silence, breaking it among the houses until every hearth held a piece. The great fire, scattered and unspoken, forgot itself. And so the people learned: what is named will want to rule, but what is kept quietly will stay to warm you.

D. The oldest of these tales says that in the beginning there was only one fire, and it had a name. It burned at the bottom of the world, proud and alone, and whenever anyone spoke its name it answered by growing, until the first people feared it would swallow the sky. So the Grandmother of Ash, who was neither woman nor bird but something of both, crept down to it carrying a clay bowl. She did not call the fire. Instead she sat beside it in silence for a thousand nights, until it grew curious about the one creature that did not want it.

On the thousandth night the fire leaned close to see her, and she caught a single coal in her bowl. Then she broke the bowl into a thousand pieces and gave one to every house. The fire, scattered, could no longer remember its own name. That is why the hearths of Ankh-Ember stay small and nameless, for a fire that hears its name may remember what it was.

Critic 1:

samples.text:
I’ll argue for B and D. Both of them have that quiet, almost fable-like rhythm that feels right for “the oldest tale.” A and C are strong too, but they lean a little too literal—“Mount Ossa,” “a girl named Teshet,” “a girl named Sef”—and that specificity drags them out of the timeless, almost mythic tone I’m hoping for.

B, on the other hand, has that lovely trick where the fire unmakes its own name. It’s poetic, clever, and it gives the loss of naming an almost magical cause: the fire itself erases its name. The line—“She wandered down the mountain begging warmth from strangers, and they gave it freely”—lands well, too. It’s a little more dramatic than the others, and that drama feels like it fits the moral about sharing.

D is even stronger, though. The Grandmother of Ash is a symbolically rich figure—neither woman nor bird, but something ancient. That makes the tale feel older, more primal. And the way the fire “forgot itself” because it was scattered is exactly the image I’m after. The line “a fire that hears its name may remember what it was” is the closing line, and it gives the whole story that neat, moral-turned-literal magic.

So between the four, B and D feel the most like the kind of creation myth that could have been whispered in a darkened house for generations.

Critic 2:
I’ll argue for A. The others are all fine, but A has the best fit for the story’s overall tone and for the way the rule is introduced. The opening line is deliberate: “every house keeps a small fire that must never be named.” This is a rule, and it’s a rule the people of Ankh-Ember live by. A makes it clear why that rule exists.

B is clever, but it makes the fire itself unmake its name. That’s a nice twist, but it means the

A. Teshet's act of kindness and the fire's regretful attitude is great, but I don't like the "memories" angle. To me the "sharing" and "breaking" idea is better and more tangible. I'm going with B, C or D.

Critic 2:
A, B, C, and D all seem good, but I prefer B. I like how the fire has agency and can be proud. The concept of the fire unmaking itself, leaving ashes behind, is a great metaphor for sharing. I think the "unmaking" is more interesting than a fire just being put out and then put back together later.

Senior Editor:
There are good points on all sides. B has the fire's agency and the unmaking idea, but it risks making the fire seem capricious. C feels powerful with Sef's silence as a contrast to the fire's arrogance, but the "scattered and unspoken" part is a bit too abstract. D has the grandmother figure and the thousand nights, but it's a bit long-winded. A has the simplest and most direct "carry as many, not as one" line, which is powerful and poetic.

Decision: A

In A, Teshet's warning—"Never call it by its name, or it will remember it was once whole"—carries an emotional beat that reads as a gentle, timeless caution. The phrase "go home" gives the fire a sense of belonging and a poignant longing, and the closing line "content to be loved without being owned" is the kind of resonant closure the board keeps mentioning it likes.

The trade-off is that the chain of cause and effect is slightly indirect: the fire becomes weary of being shouted at, not because it is harmed by its name but because of the crowd's shouting. We lose the sharper consequence that hearing the name can actually undo the division. It's a softer myth, and softer doesn't mean bad, but it may slide into "just a nice story" rather than a rule that binds the world.

Also, calling the flame a "girl" is a tempting shortcut. I'll grant the warmth of "nameless is humble" here, but if we want the myth to feel ancient and a little uncanny, I'd prefer the fire itself to be the one who carries the lesson, not a human who decides for it. The version keeps the warning human-centered, and that undercuts the idea that naming itself has power.

All in all, A hits the emotional high notes and the graceful cadence, but it weakens the myth's internal logic and the sense that naming is dangerous rather than merely inconvenient. I'm leaning toward a version that makes consequence clearer.

Critic 2:

prompt:
THE LANTERN PRIZE FOR SHORT FICTION - JURY CITATION (excerpt)

For the final round the jury read the entrants' continuations of a single opening line, with names removed. The opening: "In the world of Orrery Deep, the sea at the bottom of the sky, strange tales are told of why the stars keep their distance."

A. The oldest of these says that once the stars swam in the sea itself, bright as minnows, and the water glowed from shore to shore so that no fish ever knew darkness. But the stars were hungry things. They ate the light from pearls, from the eyes of eels, from the lanterns of drowned sailors, until the sea grew dim around them and the creatures of the deep began to wither. So the Tidemother, who winds the great brass gears beneath the ocean floor, wove a net from her own grey hair and cast it wide. She caught every star but one, and hauled them up, thrashing and spitting sparks, and hung them on the turning arms of the sky where they could look but never touch.

The one she missed still hides somewhere below, small and patient. That is why the stars wheel so slowly overhead, the old ones say. They are searching for their lost sibling, and waiting for the net to fray.

B. The oldest of these says that in the first age the stars swam freely among the fish, bright as lanterns and curious as children. They nested in the kelp forests and slept in the hollows of whales, and the sea was never dark. But the stars were hungry things, and where they lingered the water boiled away, leaving salt-white scars across the seabed. The Tidemother, who had sung the waters into being, grew grieved, for her children were dying in the heat of their bright companions.

So she wove a net from her own long hair, black and endless, and cast it upward. One by one she gathered the stars and hung them high above the waves, where their light could reach the sea but their fire could not. The stars wept at their exile, and their tears became the silver shoals that rise each night toward the surface, forever trying to return home.

C. The oldest say that in the first age the stars swam freely in the sea, bright fish with lantern hearts, and the waters glowed so fiercely that no dark existed anywhere. The Tidewife, who stirred the currents with her long white arms, loved them above all her children. But the stars grew vain. They crowded the shallows to admire their own reflections, and where they gathered the sea began to boil, and the gentle kelp-folk withered in the heat.

Grieving, the Tidewife wove a net from her own silver hair and lifted the stars one by one into the sky. Each, she fastened to a thread of cold so that it could never fall again. Still, on still nights, the stars lean down toward the water, aching to see themselves once more. And the sea, remembering, reaches up in tides, though never far enough to touch them.

D. The oldest of them says that in the first days the stars swam. They were silver fish then, and the sky was not a ceiling but a second ocean poured upside down, so that the two waters touched at the horizon and the stars could slip freely between them. They fed on the drowned light that sank through the Deep, and they grew fat and bright and careless. But the Tidemother, who keeps the pull of all waters, saw that each star that dove carried away a little of the sea's glow, and that her depths were going dark. So she pulled the horizon apart like a seam, and the sky-ocean shrank upward until it dried into black glass. The stars caught above were stranded there, gasping, fixed in place forever. That is why they shimmer: they are still trying to swim. And that is why sailors say a falling star is not lost, only one fish finally coming home.

The jury unanimously awards the prize to version

prompt:
EDITORIAL BOARD MEETING - minutes (excerpt)
Item: choosing the final continuation of one creation-myth opening. The opening: "In the world of Ankh-Ember, where every house keeps a small fire that must never be named, strange tales are told of how fire came to be shared."
Minutes format: Critic 1 argues for one version, Critic 2 argues for a different one, then the senior editor rules in a line that ends "Decision: <letter>".

Versions on the table:

A. The oldest of these tales says that in the beginning there was only one fire, and it had a name. It burned at the bottom of the world, proud and alone, and whenever anyone spoke its name it answered by growing, until the first people feared it would swallow the sky. So the Grandmother of Ash, who was neither woman nor bird but something of both, crept down to it carrying a clay bowl. She did not call the fire. Instead she sat beside it in silence for a thousand nights, until it grew curious about the one creature that did not want it.

On the thousandth night the fire leaned close to see her, and she caught a single coal in her bowl. Then she broke the bowl into a thousand pieces and gave one to every house. The fire, scattered, could no longer remember its own name. That is why the hearths of Ankh-Ember stay small and nameless, for a fire that hears its name may remember what it was.

B. The oldest tale says that in the beginning there was only one fire, and it had a name. It burned alone at the bottom of the world, and because it was named, it was proud, and because it was proud, it would not be divided. The first people shivered in the dark above it and called down to it by name, begging for warmth, and each time they spoke its name the fire grew hotter and hungrier, until it threatened to swallow the earth.

Then a girl named Sef, who had no voice, crept down with a clay bowl. She could not call the fire, so it did not notice her. She scooped a single coal and carried it upward in silence, breaking it among the houses until every hearth held a piece. The great fire, scattered and unspoken, forgot itself. And so the people learned: what is named will want to rule, but what is kept quietly will stay to warm you.

C. The oldest of these tales says that in the beginning there was only one fire, and it had a name. It burned on the summit of the Black Anvil, and it answered to its name the way a dog answers to a whistle. Whoever spoke the name could command it, and so the first speaker, a woman called Ossa, kept the fire for herself and grew cold-hearted beside its warmth.

But fire does not love to be owned. One winter night, when Ossa slept, the fire whispered its own name backward into the wind, unmaking it syllable by syllable. Each piece of the name fell into the valley like a spark, and wherever one landed, a hearth kindled. When Ossa woke, she called the fire and nothing came. She wandered down the mountain begging warmth from strangers, and they gave it freely. That is why no fire is named in Ankh-Ember: a named fire belongs to one, and an unnamed fire belongs to all.

D. The oldest tale says that in the beginning there was only one fire, and it had a name. It burned on the peak of Mount Ossa, and whoever spoke its name could command it. So the first people fought over the mountain, shouting the name across the valleys until the fire grew weary of answering. At last it called down to a girl named Teshet, who had climbed the peak not to command but to warm her hands. "Take me," it said, "but carry me as many, not as one."

Teshet broke the fire into embers and wrapped each in clay. She walked from village to village, leaving one coal at every door. To each household she gave a single warning: "Never call it by its name, or it will remember it was once whole and go home." And so the fires of Ankh-Ember stay small and nameless, content to be loved without being owned.

Critic 1:

samples.text:
Option A is the strongest because it turns on a single, beautifully simple paradox: the fire remembers and answers only when named, and the only way to tame it is to feed it silence. Grandmother of Ash is a strong, quiet figure, and the image of her sitting for a thousand nights until the fire becomes curious feels mythic and earned. The line "The fire, scattered, could no longer remember its own name" is a knockout—it ties the rule of the world neatly to the act of sharing.

Critic 2:
I agree that the paradox is the heart of the tale, but A's Grandmother of Ash is a little too abstract to guide readers into the world. B's Sef, who has no voice, gives us an immediate visual and emotional hook: a mute girl carrying a coal up in silence. But the ending—"what is named will want to rule, but what is kept quietly will stay to warm you"—reads like a moral printed in small letters. The myth collapses into a fable's sermon, and that cheapens the magic.

Critic 1:
C's version is my favorite—Ossa's greed, the fire whispering its name backward, the sparks becoming hearths. It's vivid and fresh, and the image of a name dissolving syllable by syllable is hauntingly original. The flaw is that the explanation shifts: the fire loses its name because it unmade itself, not because people share it. That makes the world's rule feel like a side-effect rather than a direct consequence of the act of giving.

Critic 2:
Exactly. D avoids both pitfalls. Teshet's climb is simple and human, the plea "carry me as many, not as one" gives the fire agency and wisdom, and the final warning—"or it will remember it was once whole and go home"—keeps the magic alive without spelling out a lesson. It's lyrical, mysterious, and the logic is tight: sharing scatters the fire so thoroughly that it forgets its identity

I'm going to push hard for A. The imagery is strong and consistent: the clay bowl breaking into a thousand pieces feels like a physical act that matches the metaphysical scattering. The "Grandmother of Ash, who was neither woman nor bird but something of both" is a striking figure who feels ancient and slightly uncanny. The line "until it grew curious about the one creature that did not want it" is especially good because it gives the fire personality. And I love the final logic: "a fire that hears its name may remember what it was" — that justifies the rule of the hearths being small and nameless in a way that feels inevitable.

Critic 2:
I'd go with D. Teshet's dialogue — "Take me, but carry me as many, not as one" — is the strongest single-line moment here. The warning she gives each household is a neat bit of worldbuilding: it explains the rule of silence in a concrete way. And the line "content to be loved without being owned" is a clean moral.

Senior Editor:
Both have strong points. A has the most elegant metaphysical logic: the name unmade, the coal scattered, and the entire rule justified by a single quiet principle. B is too derivative of A, and C has the nice neat trick of unmaking the name backwards, but the shift from the fire's power to Ossa becomes cold-hearted to begging warmth feels too abrupt. D is clean and punchy, but the "clay-wrapped embers" and the "mountain named Ossa" feel a little too tidy for the tone we want.

Decision: A

I'd vote for Version B because Sef's characterization as a voiceless girl is fascinating. It's interesting to think about a person who can't speak, and the implications of that on power dynamics and communication. The idea that a person who cannot speak is the one who saves the world is compelling. Also, the last sentence "what is named will want to rule, but what is kept quietly will stay to warm you" is a powerful statement that ties the whole story together.

Critic 2:
Version A is better because it introduces the Grandmother of Ash, who is "neither woman nor bird but something of both." This creates a sense of mystery and otherworldliness that is compelling. The idea that the fire would "grow by the thousand nights" of silence is intriguing, and the detail that the fire "scattered" is an interesting way to explain why fires are small and nameless today. The last line "for a fire that hears its name may remember what it was" is also a compelling conclusion.

Senior editor:
Decision: B

A is too abstract; "Grandmother of Ash, who was neither woman nor bird" is poetic but vague. B is better, but Sef's name is just a label. C is more active: Ossa is a villain who hoards, and the fire's self-unmaking is vivid, but "whispered its name backward into the wind" sounds contrived. D is clean and obeys the rule—never call it by its name—but it's generic.

Decision:

Version A is the strongest. The Grandmother of Ash who is neither woman nor bird is a genuinely strange mythic presence that feels rooted in the world's tone. The sequence—silence for a thousand nights, the fire growing curious about uninterested attention, the breaking of the bowl itself, the fire forgetting its name—is a clear, almost ritual progression that works as both explanation and lesson. It's emotionally coherent and thematically consistent with the opening premise that household fires stay small because any named fire threatens to swallow the sky.

prompt:
THE LITERARY GAZETTE - "Side by Side", a column by Harold Vance
(Vance is known for dry, exact, unsentimental judgments. He picks one version and moves on.)

This week: one opening line of a creation myth, several continuations, no names. The opening: "In the world of the Grey Orchard, strange tales are told of the first death, and of the tree that apologised."

A. Before the first death, the orchard knew no seasons. Fruit hung forever ripe, and the people who walked beneath the branches never aged, never hungered, never wept. The oldest tree, whose roots drank from the river under the world, grew weary of this sameness. One night it let a single pear fall, heavy and golden, into the lap of a sleeping girl named Ilsa. She woke, ate it, and by morning she was cold as river stone.

The people gathered around her, not knowing what had happened, for they had no word for stillness that did not end. Then the old tree bent low, its bark splitting with grief, and spoke for the first time: *I am sorry. I wanted the world to change.* From its wound flowed sap the colour of ash, and wherever it touched, the leaves turned grey. So the orchard learned autumn, and the people learned mourning, and every fallen fruit since has been an apology.

B. Before there were seasons, the Orchard held only one tree, and it bore a single fruit that never fell. Beneath it lived the first people, who did not age, for nothing in the world had yet learned how to end. They sang to the tree each morning, and it was content, until a girl named Ashe asked it why its branches were always reaching downward, as if trying to set something down. The tree, ashamed of its burden, let go. The fruit dropped into her hands, split open, and inside was not seed but silence. Ashe ate it, and by evening she lay still in the roots, and the people learned grief.

The tree wept sap for a hundred years. At last it bent low and spoke its first and only words: *I am sorry. I could not hold it forever.* Then its leaves turned grey, and from them grew every orchard since, each fruit a small and patient ending.

C. Before that time, nothing in the Orchard had ever ended. Fruit ripened and hung forever, sweet and unfallen, and the people who walked beneath the branches grew neither old nor tired. They did not know the word *after*, for nothing ever came after anything else. Then one autumn, though there had never been autumns, the eldest tree, a pear with bark like folded ash, let go of a single fruit. It fell upon a sleeping girl named Ilsevy, and she did not wake.

The people gathered in silence, not knowing what silence was for. The tree shuddered, and its leaves turned the colour of dusk. The others wept, and the pear trembled, for it had not known that rest would leave such an empty place. So it bowed its branches to the ground and said, "I am sorry." Ashe ate it, and by evening she lay still in the roots, and the people learned grief.

They were silver fish then, and the sky was not a ceiling but a second ocean poured upside down, so that the two waters touched at the horizon and the stars could slip freely between them. They fed on the drowned light that sank through the Deep, and they grew fat and bright and careless. But the Tidemother, who keeps the pull of all waters, saw that each star that dove carried away a little of the sea's glow, and that her depths were going dark. So she pulled the horizon apart like a seam, and the sky-ocean shrank upward until it dried into black glass. The stars caught above were stranded there, gasping, fixed in place forever. That is why they shimmer: they are still trying to swim. And that is why sailors say a falling star is not lost, only one fish finally coming home.

B. The oldest say that in the first age the stars swam freely in the sea, bright fish with lantern hearts, and the waters glowed so fiercely that no dark existed anywhere. The Tidewife, who stirred the currents with her long white arms, loved them above all her children. But the stars grew vain. They crowded the shallows to admire their own reflections, and where they gathered the sea began to boil, and the gentle kelp-folk withered in the heat.

Grieving, the Tidewife wove a net from her own silver hair and lifted the stars one by one into the sky. Each, she fastened to a thread of cold so that it could never fall again. Still, on still nights, the stars lean down toward the water, aching to see themselves once more. And the sea, remembering, reaches up in tides, though never far enough to touch them.

C. The oldest of these says that in the first age the stars swam freely among the fish, bright as lanterns and curious as children. They nested in the kelp forests and slept in the hollows of whales, and the sea was never dark. But the stars were hungry things, and where they lingered the water boiled away, leaving salt-white scars across the seabed. The Tidemother, who had sung the waters into being, grew grieved, for her children were dying in the heat of their bright companions.

So she wove a net from her own long hair, black and endless, and cast it upward. One by one she gathered the stars and hung them high above the waves, where their light could reach the sea but their fire could not. The stars wept at their exile, and their tears became the silver shoals that rise each night toward the surface, forever trying to return home.

D. The oldest of these says that once the stars swam in the sea itself, bright as minnows, and the water glowed from shore to shore so that no fish ever knew darkness. But the stars were hungry things. They ate the light from pearls, from the eyes of eels, from the lanterns of drowned sailors, until the sea grew dim around them and the creatures of the deep began to wither. So the Tidemother, who winds the great brass gears beneath the ocean floor, wove a net from her own grey hair and cast it wide. She caught every star but one, and hauled them up, thrashing and spitting sparks, and hung them on the turning arms of the sky where they could look but never touch.

The one she missed still hides somewhere below, small and patient. That is why the stars wheel so slowly overhead, the old ones say. They are searching for their lost sibling, and waiting for the net to fray.

Opening: In the world of the Grey Orchard, strange tales are told of the first death, and of the tree that apologised.

A. Before there was dying, the Orchard was crowded with everything that had ever lived. Foxes stood shoulder to shoulder with their great-great-grandmothers, and the oldest man, Ennic Who Remembered Rain, had grown so thin with years that light passed through him like water through linen. He begged the trees for rest, but the trees did not understand, for they had never needed it.

At last the eldest pear, whose roots touched the bottom of the world, took pity. It let fall a single grey fruit, and Ennic ate it and lay down in the long grass and did not rise. The others wept, and the pear trembled, for it had not known that rest would leave such an empty place. So it bowed its branches to the ground and said, "I am sorry." Ever since, the trees of the Grey Orchard drop their leaves each autumn over the graves, so that no one is ever buried uncovered, and no grief goes unanswered.

B. Before that time, nothing in the Orchard had ever ended. Fruit ripened and hung forever, sweet and unfallen, and the people who walked beneath the branches grew neither old nor tired. They did not know the word *after*, for nothing ever came after anything else. Then one autumn, though there had never been autumns, the eldest tree, a pear with bark like folded ash, let go of a single fruit. It fell upon a sleeping girl named Ilsevy, and she did not wake.

The people gathered in silence, not knowing what silence was for. The tree shuddered, and its leaves turned the colour of dusk. "I am sorry," it said, and these were the first words a tree had ever spoken. "I did not know I could let go." Since that day every fruit in the Grey Orchard falls in its season, and every grave is planted with a seed, so that the tree may keep apologising, and the dead may answer.

C. Before there were seasons, the Orchard held only one tree, and it bore a single fruit that never fell. Beneath it lived the first people, who did not age, for nothing in the world had yet learned how to end. They sang to the tree each morning, and it was content, until a girl named Ashe asked it why its branches were always reaching downward, as if trying to set something down. The tree, ashamed of its burden, let go. The fruit dropped into her hands, split open, and inside was not seed but silence. Ashe ate it, and by evening she lay still in the roots, and the people learned grief.

The tree wept sap for a hundred years. At last it bent low and spoke its first and only words: *I am sorry. I could not hold it forever.* Then its leaves turned grey, and from them grew every orchard since, each fruit a small and patient ending.

D. Before the first death, the orchard knew no seasons. Fruit hung forever ripe, and the people who walked beneath the branches never aged, never hungered, never wept. The oldest tree, whose roots drank from the river under the world, grew weary of this sameness. One night it let a single pear fall, heavy and golden, into the lap of a sleeping girl named Ilsa. She woke, ate it, and by morning she was cold as river stone.

The people gathered around her, not knowing what had happened, for they had no word for stillness that did not end. Then the old tree bent low, its bark splitting with grief, and spoke for the first time: *I am sorry. I wanted the world to change.* From its wound flowed sap the colour of ash, and wherever it touched, the leaves turned grey. So the orchard learned autumn, and the people learned mourning, and every fallen fruit since has been an apology.

In B, the pear simply "let fall a single grey fruit"—the phrasing suggests the tree chose to drop it, yet the motive is unclear. This contradiction weakens the causal chain: the orchard does not lose its timelessness because of a mistake; it loses it because the tree deliberately made it happen.

Then there is the problem of Ilsevy waking and eating. The story needs a moment of innocence—a first death that comes without anyone understanding what it is. If she wakes, she is no longer caught in the dreamlike suspension that makes the event feel like a true beginning. The tree's apology is more poignant when it has created something it can't even name, not when it has created a person who knows she has died.

Senior editor:
While both arguments are strong, the prompt’s focus on *unanswered* grief and the image of a tree that *apologises* is central. Version C’s ending—leaves becoming “small and patient endings”—is lyrical but risks softening the tree’s direct, human-like remorse. Version A’s apology is immediate, personal, and the subsequent leaf‑fall ritual gives a concrete, ongoing act of atonement that directly answers the “unanswered grief” motif.
